entry.title: Debugging an Off-Grid Solar Lighting System: Understanding Common Failure Points
entry.summary: Off-grid solar lighting systems look simple: a solar panel collects energy, a battery stores it, and an LED provides lighting at night. However, when the system stops working, the problem is usually not caused by one single component. The failure may come from the interaction between power generation, energy storage, control logic, and the final load. A basic solar lighting system usually works like this: When troubleshooting, it is important to check the system step by step instead of replacing parts randomly. The first thing to confirm is the LED load itself. A damaged LED module, internal circuit issue, or loose connection can prevent the light from operating. If the LED is working properly, the next area to check is the battery. Since the battery stores energy for nighttime operation, reduced capacity, aging, or insufficient charging can cause the system to fail after sunset. The solar input should then be inspected. Dust, shading, damaged panels, or poor connections can reduce charging performance and gradually lead to nighttime failures. For outdoor systems, wiring and sensors should also be checked. Exposure to rain, humidity, and temperature changes can cause connection problems over time. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: The same approach can be applied to many other off-grid electronic systems. Understanding how energy flows through the entire system is often more effective than focusing on individual components. Reliable hardware depends not only on good components, but also on proper system integration and maintenance.

entry.title: Your AI agent works great. Then the phone gets warm. Then it doesn’t.
entry.summary: There’s a failure mode in on-device AI agents that doesn’t show up in testing. It shows up five minutes into a real session. The device gets warm. The CPU downclocks. Latency spikes. The agent that responded in 200ms is now taking 800ms. Users don’t report “thermal throttling” — they report “it got slow” or “it stopped working.” By the time you’re debugging, it looks like a model problem. It’s not. What’s actually happening Android’s thermal system throttles CPU and GPU frequency when the device temperature rises. Continuous inference — running a model repeatedly over several minutes — generates heat. On flagship devices with good thermal management, you might not notice. On a mid-range device from two years ago, you will. PowerManager.getThermalHeadroom() gives you a 1-second forecast of …
